10  Pose Rules

Each rule below states one behaviour and shows it on a rendered pose, with the printed structure where the shape is the point.

The rules are organized into seven sections (Construction, Layer Placement, Inferred Columns, Scope, Options, Assembly, Layout) and cover the call shapes of pj/pose, pj/lay-*, pj/arrange, pj/options, pj/scale, pj/coord, and pj/facet.

Read Poses first. On a first read through the book you can skim or skip this chapter, and return when you want the precise rule behind a behavior.

(ns plotje-book.pose-rules
  (:require
   ;; Kindly -- notebook rendering protocol
   [scicloj.kindly.v4.kind :as kind]
   ;; Tablecloth -- dataset operations
   [tablecloth.api :as tc]
   ;; Rdatasets -- standard datasets
   [scicloj.metamorph.ml.rdatasets :as rdatasets]
   ;; Plotje -- composable plotting
   [scicloj.plotje.api :as pj]))

Setup

(def iris (rdatasets/datasets-iris))

A helper to inspect pose structure without :data – the dataset is heavy and not what we are checking. We strip :data from the pose and every nested sub-pose and layer.

(defn strip-data [pose]
  (cond-> (dissoc pose :data)
    (:layers pose) (update :layers (partial mapv #(dissoc % :data)))
    (:poses pose) (update :poses (partial mapv strip-data))))
(defn pose-summary
  "Print pose structure without :data (for readability)."
  [pose]
  (kind/pprint (strip-data pose)))

The cells of a composite – its leaves, in reading order. pj/arrange puts its cells in rows, so they are not its :poses directly.

(defn cells [pose]
  (filterv #(not (contains? % :poses)) (rest (tree-seq :poses :poses pose))))

Overview

A pose is a plain Clojure map with a documented set of keys:

Key On Purpose
:data leaf or any ancestor dataset (Tablecloth)
:mapping pose or layer column-to-aesthetic bindings
:layers pose per-scope layers
:poses composite only sub-poses
:layout composite direction + weights
:facet leaf a facet over columns, expanded into cells when the pose is drawn (Rule O3)
:opts root plot-level options (incl. composite-level keys like :share-scales)
:share-scales composite the axes the cells share; pj/arrange writes it under :opts, and pj/marginal writes it on the composite itself
:where any pose a map from a column to a value or a set of values; the pose draws only the rows that match

A leaf pose has :data, :mapping, :layers; no :poses. A composite pose has :poses, and a sub-pose may itself be a composite: pj/arrange wraps its cells in a row per line of the grid, so the composite it returns holds rows and each row holds cells. A composite the caller supplies is accepted the same way: pj/arrange given one among its inputs nests it (Rule C8), pj/facet called on one divides every cell of it (Rule O3), and a nested map written out and handed to pj/pose is read as written. So a grid inside a grid can be written directly. A layer is a map with :layer-type and an optional :mapping, plus sibling keys :stat, :position, :mark when the user provides them.

Construction

How poses and composites come into existence. Nine rules covering every pj/pose call shape plus pj/arrange.

Rule C1: pj/pose on raw data creates a leaf

Called with a dataset as first argument, pj/pose returns a leaf pose. The arity determines what’s in :mapping: a keyword is :x; two keywords are :x and :y; a final map is the mapping and contributes aesthetic keys.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width))
(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pose-summary)
{:mapping {:x :sepal-length, :y :sepal-width}, :layers []}

With only :color in the mapping, the pose is a leaf that names no :x and no :y. On data of one to three columns, the columns are read by default when the pose is drawn (Rule LI1). Iris has more columns, so a layer added to this pose has to name its columns, or a later pj/pose call has to name them.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose {:color :species})
    pose-summary)
{:mapping {:color :species}, :layers []}

Rule C2: pj/pose on a leaf merges into its mapping

pj/pose called on a leaf merges the new mapping into the leaf’s own mapping, whatever the leaf or its layers already name. The leaf remains a leaf, and no composite is created.

(-> iris
    pj/pose
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width))

And an aesthetic-on-aesthetic extension merges with later-wins:

(-> iris
    (pj/pose {:color :species})
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width))

Property P-C2 – construction commutativity. A mapping built over several pj/pose calls is equal to the same mapping written in one call.

(= (-> iris
       pj/pose
       (pj/pose {:color :species})
       (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width))
   (pj/pose iris :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species}))
true

Rule C3: pj/pose naming other columns replaces the leaf’s :x and :y

pj/pose writes one mapping and does not add a panel. Called with an :x or :y other than the one the leaf’s mapping has, it replaces that column, and the layers that name no columns of their own read the new columns. So a pose returned by a function can be pointed at other columns:

(defn trend-plot [data]
  (-> data
      (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
      pj/lay-point
      pj/lay-smooth))
(-> (trend-plot iris)
    (pj/pose :petal-length :petal-width))
Notestdout 
Note: on this pose, pj/pose replaces :x :sepal-length with :petal-length and :y :sepal-width with :petal-width; in 0.16.1 it added a panel. For panels side by side, write (pj/arrange data [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}]).

(-> (trend-plot iris)
    (pj/pose :petal-length :petal-width)
    pose-summary)
Notestdout 
Note: on this pose, pj/pose replaces :x :sepal-length with :petal-length and :y :sepal-width with :petal-width; in 0.16.1 it added a panel. For panels side by side, write (pj/arrange data [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}]).

{:mapping {:x :petal-length, :y :petal-width},
 :layers [{:layer-type :point} {:layer-type :smooth}]}

A layer that names its own columns keeps them. The pose’s new :x and :y are then drawn by no layer, and drawing the pose prints a warning naming them:

(-> iris
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/pose :petal-length :petal-width))

For panels side by side, pj/arrange takes a cell for each panel, here a mapping naming the panel’s two columns:

(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
    pj/lay-point)

Property P-C3 – writing the same columns again changes nothing. A pj/pose call naming the leaf’s own :x and :y returns the same pose.

(= (trend-plot iris)
   (pj/pose (trend-plot iris) :sepal-length :sepal-width))
true

Rule C4: pj/pose with no :x or :y merges into the leaf’s mapping

A pj/pose call naming no :x and no :y, on a leaf whose mapping names them, merges the aesthetic into the leaf’s :mapping. The leaf stays a leaf.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/pose {:color :species}))
(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/pose {:color :species})
    pose-summary)
{:mapping {:x :sepal-length, :y :sepal-width, :color :species},
 :layers []}

Property P-C4 – the aesthetic may come in a second call. Adding the aesthetic in a second call equals writing it in the first.

(= (-> iris
       (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
       (pj/pose {:color :species}))
   (pj/pose iris :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species}))
true

Rule C5: pj/pose leaves the layers where they are

pj/pose changes only the mapping. The layers stay on the pose they were added to, and a layer that names no columns of its own reads the merged mapping.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/pose {:color :species}))
(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/pose {:color :species})
    pose-summary)
{:mapping {:x :sepal-length, :y :sepal-width, :color :species},
 :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}

Rule C6: pj/pose on a composite merges into the root mapping

On a composite, pj/pose merges into the root :mapping, which reaches every cell that does not map the same aesthetic itself. So an aesthetic that no cell maps itself reaches every cell:

(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
    (pj/pose {:color :species})
    pj/lay-point)
(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
    (pj/pose {:color :species})
    pj/lay-point
    pose-summary)
{:mapping {:color :species},
 :layout {:direction :vertical, :cols :auto},
 :poses
 [{:layout {:direction :horizontal},
   :poses
   [{:mapping {:x :sepal-length, :y :sepal-width}, :layers []}
    {:mapping {:x :petal-length, :y :petal-width}, :layers []}]}],
 :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}

An :x or a :y written on a composite whose cells each name their own :x and :y reaches none of the cells. The cells keep their columns, and drawing the pose prints a warning for each axis, saying that the column written on the composite is not drawn:

(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :petal-length)
    pj/lay-point)

Rule C7: pj/pose with nothing new has no effect

(pj/pose pose) and (pj/pose pose {}), where pose is a leaf or a composite, return pose unchanged, and writing a mapping twice gives the pose that writing it once gives. So pj/pose is safe to use as a pipeline step that does nothing.

A leaf pose. First the rendered plot, then its structure:

(def leaf-pose (-> iris (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)))
leaf-pose
(pose-summary leaf-pose)
{:mapping {:x :sepal-length, :y :sepal-width}, :layers []}

Wrapping it with pj/pose returns the same value:

(= leaf-pose
   (pj/pose leaf-pose)
   (pj/pose leaf-pose {}))
true
(= (pj/pose leaf-pose {:color :species})
   (pj/pose (pj/pose leaf-pose {:color :species}) {:color :species}))
true

A composite pose. The rendered plot, then its structure:

(def composite-pose
  (-> iris
      (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
      pj/lay-point))
composite-pose
(pose-summary composite-pose)
{:layout {:direction :vertical, :cols :auto},
 :poses
 [{:layout {:direction :horizontal},
   :poses
   [{:mapping {:x :sepal-length, :y :sepal-width}, :layers []}
    {:mapping {:x :petal-length, :y :petal-width}, :layers []}]}],
 :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}

And again, pj/pose has no effect:

(= composite-pose
   (pj/pose composite-pose)
   (pj/pose composite-pose {}))
true

Rule C8: pj/arrange composes poses into a composite

pj/arrange returns a composite. It takes a vector of cells, or data or a pose first and then the cells. A cell is what one argument after the data is to pj/pose: a pose, a composite, a column (a panel of that column), or a mapping such as {:x :a :y :b} (a panel of the columns the mapping names). So a cell and (pj/pose nil cell) draw the same. nil is the exception: in pj/arrange it is a cell left empty, where after the data in pj/pose it names no column. A vector is never a cell. A vector in the cell list is a list of cells: a row, where the cell list is a list of rows, and otherwise an arrangement of its own. The cells are placed in rows: the composite’s :poses are the rows, and each row’s :poses are the cells of that row.

(pj/arrange
 [(-> iris (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width) pj/lay-point)
  (-> iris (pj/pose :petal-length :petal-width) pj/lay-point)])

A cell may itself be a composite, and nests rather than being flattened – which is the shape pj/arrange builds for itself, one row per line of the grid:

(-> (pj/arrange [(pj/arrange [(pj/pose iris :sepal-length :sepal-width)
                              (pj/pose iris :petal-length :petal-width)])
                 (pj/pose iris :sepal-length :petal-length)])
    pj/lay-point)

Given data first, a list of vectors of columns is a list of rows, with a panel for each column, as a list of vectors of poses is:

(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [[:sepal-length :sepal-width] [:petal-length :petal-width]])
    pj/lay-histogram)

pj/arrange writes the options it is given into the composite’s :opts: :title, :width, :height, :share-scales, and any plot option pj/options takes. :cols decides how many cells each row holds, and is written on the composite’s :layout rather than its :opts: an arrangement made from a flat list keeps it there, as :auto where no :cols was given, so that cells appended later are laid out as one call with the longer list lays them out.

(pj/arrange
 [(pj/pose iris :sepal-length :sepal-width)
  (pj/pose iris :petal-length :sepal-width)]
 {:title "Arranged"
  :share-scales #{:y}})

Rule C9: a facet crossing two lists of columns is a leaf pose

pj/facet given the map that crosses two lists of columns, {:col {:x cols} :row {:y cols}}, keeps that map on a leaf pose – no :poses – which the facet splits into a panel for every pair when the pose is drawn. A mapping written on the pose reaches every panel.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose {:color :species})
    (pj/facet {:col {:x [:sepal-length :sepal-width]}
              :row {:y [:sepal-length :sepal-width]}}))

Property P-C9 – the mapping can come first or last. A mapping written with pj/pose before the facet or after it gives an equal pose.

(let [a (-> iris
            (pj/pose {:color :species})
            (pj/facet {:col {:x [:sepal-length :sepal-width]}
                       :row {:y [:sepal-length :sepal-width]}}))
      b (-> iris
            (pj/facet {:col {:x [:sepal-length :sepal-width]}
                       :row {:y [:sepal-length :sepal-width]}})
            (pj/pose {:color :species}))]
  (= a b))
true

Layer Placement

Where lay-* calls place the layer in the pose tree. The rules cover whether the call names :x and :y, whether the receiver is a leaf or a composite, the raw-data convenience case, the panel the layers of a leaf share, and the columns a layer reads from that panel.

Where the columns are written: the columns a lay-* call names are written on the layer’s own :mapping, and only there; the pose’s :mapping is what pj/pose writes. The two meet by scope merge when the pose is drawn: a layer that names a column overrides the pose’s, and a layer that names none reads the pose’s.

Rule LP1: bare lay-* attaches at the current pose’s root

A lay-* call naming no columns attaches the layer to the current pose’s top-level :layers. On a leaf, that is the leaf’s own :layers. On a composite, it is the root :layers, and the layer flows into every descendant leaf when rendered.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pj/lay-point)

On a composite, the same call attaches at root and reaches every panel when rendered:

(-> (pj/arrange
     [(pj/pose iris :sepal-length :sepal-width)
      (pj/pose iris :petal-length :petal-width)])
    pj/lay-point)
(-> (pj/arrange
     [(pj/pose iris :sepal-length :sepal-width)
      (pj/pose iris :petal-length :petal-width)])
    pj/lay-point
    pose-summary)
{:layout {:direction :vertical, :cols :auto},
 :poses
 [{:layout {:direction :horizontal},
   :poses
   [{:mapping {:x :sepal-length, :y :sepal-width}, :layers []}
    {:mapping {:x :petal-length, :y :petal-width}, :layers []}]}],
 :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}

Property P-LP1 – bare layers flow downward. After adding one bare layer to a composite, the composite’s root :layers holds that single entry. Each cell whose number of columns the layer type draws from draws the root’s layer first, underneath the cell’s own layers, and a cell that draws the root’s layer has no layer inferred for it.

(let [before (pj/arrange
              [(pj/pose iris :sepal-length :sepal-width)
               (pj/pose iris :petal-length :petal-width)])
      after  (-> (pj/arrange
                  [(pj/pose iris :sepal-length :sepal-width)
                   (pj/pose iris :petal-length :petal-width)])
                 pj/lay-point)]
  [(count (or (:layers before) []))
   (count (or (:layers after)  []))])
[0 1]

Rule LP2: on a composite, a lay-* naming columns attaches to the last matching leaf

When a lay-* call names :x and :y on a composite, and the panel of at least one leaf draws those two columns, the layer attaches to the last such leaf in left-to-right depth-first order. The columns of a leaf’s panel are the :x and :y of the leaf’s mapping after the mappings above the leaf are merged in; where that mapping names no column on an axis, the panel’s column on that axis is the column of the leaf’s first layer that names a column there. The layer’s own :mapping carries the columns the call named. This is the same “most recent matching leaf” rule the teaching chapters describe, formalized for composite poses where reading-order depth-first traversal gives the precise answer. Matching is by strict equality: a column reference is the keyword or string the user typed, and the two forms are not interchangeable.

(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width))

A cell built by lay-* names its columns on its layer and not in its own mapping. The panel’s columns are the same either way, so the layer attaches to that cell too:

(-> (pj/arrange [(pj/lay-point iris :sepal-length :sepal-width)
                 (pj/lay-point iris :petal-length :petal-width)])
    (pj/lay-smooth :petal-length :petal-width))

Note on leaf-input with other columns. A leaf that already carries columns, called with a lay-* that names different columns, keeps the layer with the columns the call named written on it. The pose stays a leaf, and the layer is drawn on the leaf’s one panel – see Rule LP5. The pose’s own columns are drawn only by layers that name none, so here only the petal columns are drawn, and drawing the pose prints a warning that the pose’s :x and :y are drawn by no layer:

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width))
Notestdout 
Note: pj/lay-point names :petal-length on :x and :petal-width on :y where this pose draws :sepal-length on :x and :sepal-width on :y, and is drawn on the same panel; in 0.16.1 it was given a panel of its own. For a panel per pair of columns, write (pj/facet pose {:x [:sepal-length :petal-length] :y [:sepal-width :petal-width]}), or arrange separate poses with pj/arrange.

Where the columns are written does not change the rule. A layer names its columns either in the call’s argument slots or in its mapping, and placement reads both alike: (pj/lay-line pose :sepal-length :petal-width) and (pj/lay-line pose {:x :sepal-length :y :petal-width}) land on the same leaf. A written value is not a column – it places a mark at that value – and the layer’s data decides which of the two a value is.

Two lines over one :x, each naming its own :y in its mapping, therefore draw on one panel, the y axis covering both columns:

(-> {:X [1 2 3 4 5] :Y [1 2 3 4 5] :Z [1 4 9 16 25]}
    (pj/pose :X)
    (pj/lay-line {:y :Y})
    (pj/lay-line {:y :Z}))
Notestdout 
Note: pj/lay-line names :Z on :y where this pose draws :Y on :y, and is drawn on the same panel; in 0.16.1 it was given a panel of its own. For a panel per column, write (pj/facet pose {:y [:Y :Z]}), or arrange separate poses with pj/arrange.

A written value in the same slot places a label. Here :x and :y are numbers on a dataset that has no column named 2, so the label is drawn at 2 and 4:

(-> {:X [1 2 3 4 5] :Y [1 2 3 4 5] :Z [1 4 9 16 25]}
    (pj/lay-point :X :Y)
    (pj/lay-text {:x 2 :y 4 :text "a note"}))

Rule LP3: on a composite, a lay-* naming columns no leaf draws appends a new leaf

When a lay-* call names :x and :y and the panel of no leaf draws those two columns, a new leaf is appended to the composite. It holds the one layer, and the layer’s own :mapping carries the columns the call named. On an arrangement made from a flat list of cells, the new leaf joins that list, and the arrangement is laid out as one pj/arrange call with the longer list would lay it out: here the new leaf joins the row as its third cell. A leaf given other columns stays a leaf instead, and its layers share its panel – see LP2 above.

(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :petal-length))

The new leaf reads the data of the composite’s root. Where the cells carry their own data and the root has none, the new leaf has no data to read: it draws a panel reading “no data”, and the call prints a Note. The Note names the columns the cells draw, for a layer meant for one of the cells, and shows the call with {:data data}, for a layer meant for a cell of its own.

(def cells-with-their-own-data
  (pj/arrange [(pj/lay-point iris :sepal-length :sepal-width)
               (pj/lay-point iris :petal-length :petal-width)]))
(with-out-str
  (pj/lay-smooth cells-with-their-own-data :sepal-length :petal-length))
"Note: pj/lay-smooth names :sepal-length and :petal-length, and no cell of this pose draws those columns, so the layer is drawn on a cell of its own. That cell has no data: the cells carry their own, and the pose they are arranged in has none. To draw the layer on a cell, name that cell's columns (the cells draw :sepal-length / :sepal-width, :petal-length / :petal-width). To keep the new cell, pass its data: (pj/lay-smooth pose :sepal-length :petal-length {:data data}).\n"

Passing the data on the call gives the new leaf its own:

(pj/lay-smooth cells-with-their-own-data :sepal-length :petal-length
               {:data iris})

Property: a split and an arrangement draw the same panels. Two layers on different columns, split over those columns with pj/facet, and the same layers attached to a composite built with pj/arrange (LP2 sends each to its matching cell) draw the same panels with the same marks. The pose values differ: the facet keeps one leaf and expands it into cells when it is drawn, while pj/arrange builds a composite.

(let [via-facet (-> iris
                    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
                    (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width)
                    (pj/facet {:x [:sepal-length :petal-length]
                               :y [:sepal-width :petal-width]}))
      via-arrange (-> iris
                      (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
                      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
                      (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width))
      drawn (fn [pose] (select-keys (pj/svg-summary pose) [:panels :points]))]
  {:via-facet-drawn (drawn via-facet)
   :via-arrange-drawn (drawn via-arrange)
   :via-facet-shape (if (:poses via-facet) :composite :leaf)
   :via-arrange-shape (if (:poses via-arrange) :composite :leaf)})
Notestdout 
Note: pj/lay-point names :petal-length on :x and :petal-width on :y where this pose draws :sepal-length on :x and :sepal-width on :y, and is drawn on the same panel; in 0.16.1 it was given a panel of its own. For a panel per pair of columns, write (pj/facet pose {:x [:sepal-length :petal-length] :y [:sepal-width :petal-width]}), or arrange separate poses with pj/arrange.

{:via-facet-drawn {:panels 2, :points 300},
 :via-arrange-drawn {:panels 2, :points 300},
 :via-facet-shape :leaf,
 :via-arrange-shape :composite}

Property: column-existence safety check. When a lay-* call names a column on an axis where the pose already draws another column, it first checks that those columns exist in the data the layer would draw from – the layer’s own :data if present, otherwise the inherited data. A missing column is almost always a typing mistake, so the call reports it at once, with the columns the data has. A first lay-* call on raw data is not checked at the call; a missing column there is reported when the pose is drawn.

The check at the call covers the columns written in the argument slots. A name written in the layer’s mapping may be a column or a value, which the data decides when the pose is drawn, so a name there that matches no column is reported when the pose is drawn.

(try
  (-> iris
      (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
      (pj/lay-point :nope :nada))
  (catch clojure.lang.ExceptionInfo e
    (ex-message e)))
"pj/lay-point :x :nope names a column that doesn't exist in the data the layer would draw from. Available columns: [:petal-length :petal-width :rownames :sepal-length :sepal-width :species]. If you meant another dataset, pass `:data` on this lay-* call."

Supplying :data on the lay-* call satisfies the safety check: the layer draws its own data, on the leaf’s panel.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/lay-point :foo :bar
                  {:data (tc/dataset {:foo [1 2 3] :bar [4 5 6]})}))
Notestdout 
Note: pj/lay-point names :foo on :x and :bar on :y where this pose draws :sepal-length on :x and :sepal-width on :y, and is drawn on the same panel; in 0.16.1 it was given a panel of its own. For a panel per pair of columns, write (pj/facet pose {:x [:sepal-length :foo] :y [:sepal-width :bar]}), or arrange separate poses with pj/arrange.

Rule LP4: lay-* on raw data coerces the data into a leaf pose

lay-* called with a dataset as its first argument coerces the data into a leaf pose first, then applies the layer. The result draws what (-> data (pj/pose :x :y) pj/lay-point) draws. This keeps the convenience one-liner (-> data (pj/lay-point :x :y)) working as the shortest path from data to plot.

(def tiny
  {:a [1 2 3 4 5]
   :b [2 4 3 5 4]})
(-> tiny
    (pj/lay-point :a :b))

The explicit two-step form draws the same plot. The two poses differ in where the columns are written: the lay-* call above keeps them on its layer, and here pj/pose writes them on the pose, where every layer added afterwards reads them:

(-> tiny
    (pj/pose :a :b)
    pj/lay-point
    pose-summary)
{:mapping {:x :a, :y :b}, :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}

nil in place of the data, followed by columns or a mapping, is a template, as it is for pj/pose: a leaf pose holding the layer and no data, completed by pj/with-data or by an arrangement given data first. nil alone reports an error.

(pj/lay-point nil :a :b)

Rule LP5: the layers of a leaf share its panel

A leaf draws one panel, and every layer on it draws there, whatever columns it names. Its :x and :y stay on the layer’s own :mapping, and the leaf’s :mapping is left as it was.

Each axis is titled by every column drawn on it. A layer with no :color specified, on the pose or on the layer, also takes a colour and a legend entry naming its columns by default, unless a layer of the panel is coloured by a column. Each layer below specifies its colour, so no colour and no legend entry is added.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color "#377eb8"})
    (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width {:color "#e6550d"}))
Notestdout 
Note: pj/lay-point names :petal-length on :x and :petal-width on :y where this pose draws :sepal-length on :x and :sepal-width on :y, and is drawn on the same panel; in 0.16.1 it was given a panel of its own. For a panel per pair of columns, write (pj/facet pose {:x [:sepal-length :petal-length] :y [:sepal-width :petal-width]}), or arrange separate poses with pj/arrange.

One panel with the blue sepal points and the orange petal points on it, each axis titled by both of its columns, and their domains stretched to hold the petal values too. Printed, the leaf’s :mapping is untouched and the petal columns sit on the second layer:

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color "#377eb8"})
    (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width {:color "#e6550d"})
    pose-summary)
Notestdout 
Note: pj/lay-point names :petal-length on :x and :petal-width on :y where this pose draws :sepal-length on :x and :sepal-width on :y, and is drawn on the same panel; in 0.16.1 it was given a panel of its own. For a panel per pair of columns, write (pj/facet pose {:x [:sepal-length :petal-length] :y [:sepal-width :petal-width]}), or arrange separate poses with pj/arrange.

{:mapping {:x :sepal-length, :y :sepal-width},
 :layers
 [{:layer-type :point,
   :mapping {:x :sepal-length, :y :sepal-width, :color "#377eb8"}}
  {:layer-type :point,
   :mapping {:x :petal-length, :y :petal-width, :color "#e6550d"}}]}

On a composite, LP3 still applies: a layer naming columns no cell draws is a cell of its own.

(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color "#377eb8"})
    (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width {:color "#e6550d"})
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-width :petal-width {:color "#4daf4a"}))

Separate panels for the layers of one leaf come from a split, (pj/facet pose {:x [...] :y [...]}), or from pj/arrange. Asking for them with {:overlay false} or (pj/overlay pose false) reports an error naming both:

(try
  (-> iris
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
      (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width {:overlay false}))
  (catch clojure.lang.ExceptionInfo e
    (ex-message e)))
"pj/lay-point -- :overlay is retired. The layers of a pose share one panel. To draw layers on separate panels, split the pose over the columns, as in (pj/facet pose {:y [:a :b]}), or give each layer a pose of its own and arrange the poses with pj/arrange."

Rule LP6: a layer reads the panel’s column where it needs one

The panel’s column on an axis is the column the pose names there, and where the pose names none, the column of the first layer that names one there. A layer reads the panel’s column on an axis where it names none and its layer type needs one: both columns for a layer naming none, and the other column for a layer naming one whose layer type draws from two.

(-> iris
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/lay-line {:y :petal-width})
    pj/lay-smooth)
Notestdout 
Note: pj/lay-line names :petal-width on :y where this pose draws :sepal-width on :y, and is drawn on the same panel; in 0.16.1 it was given a panel of its own. For a panel per column, write (pj/facet pose {:y [:sepal-width :petal-width]}), or arrange separate poses with pj/arrange.

The columns stay on the layers. The pose’s own mapping is not written, so a layer type that can draw from one column reads no second column from a neighbouring layer:

(-> iris
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/lay-rug {:x :petal-length})
    pj/draft
    :layers
    second
    (select-keys [:mark :x :y]))
Notestdout 
Note: pj/lay-rug names :petal-length on :x where this pose draws :sepal-length on :x, and is drawn on the same panel; in 0.16.1 it was given a panel of its own. For a panel per column, write (pj/facet pose {:x [:sepal-length :petal-length]}), or arrange separate poses with pj/arrange.

{:mark :rug, :x :petal-length}

Inferred Columns

Which columns a pose draws when no column names are written. One rule. (How column references are compared is covered by Rule LP2.)

Rule LI1: few-column datasets infer columns from column order

When lay-* or pj/pose is called on a dataset without explicit column arguments, the mapping is read off the order of the dataset’s columns when the pose is drawn:

Columns Inferred mapping
1 {:x col0}
2 {:x col0 :y col1}
3 {:x col0 :y col1 :color col2}
4+ none (name the columns)

The example is a dataset rather than a map literal, because the rule reads an order and a Clojure map does not carry one.

(-> (tc/dataset {:height [1 2 3] :weight [4 5 6] :species ["a" "b" "a"]})
    pj/lay-point)

With four or more columns no column is read by default. The pj/lay-point call returns a pose, and a later step may name the columns:

(-> (tc/dataset {:a [1 2] :b [3 4] :c [5 6] :d [7 8]})
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/pose {:x :a :y :b}))

Drawn with no column named, the pose reports an error naming the layer and the columns of the data:

(try
  (-> (tc/dataset {:a [1 2] :b [3 4] :c [5 6] :d [7 8]})
      pj/lay-point
      pj/plan)
  (catch Exception e
    (ex-message e)))
"pj/lay-point draws from two columns, one on :x and one on :y, and this layer has no column on :x or :y. It names no column. Name both on the layer -- (pj/lay-point pose :x-column :y-column) -- or in the pose's mapping, which every layer of the pose reads. The data has 4 columns, so none is read by default. Available columns: [:a :b :c :d]"

Scope

How mappings, data and row filters flow through the pose tree: from the root, through each composite, to the leaf and its layers, at any depth.

Where two values for one key meet – a later pj/pose on the same pose, a layer under its pose, a cell under its composite – they combine the same way at every level. A key holds either one value, which the later or inner value replaces, or a map of independent settings, which combines key by key: a scale spec (Rule S6), a row filter (Rule S5), a :theme (Rule O5).

Rule S1: mapping scope is a tree-walk merge; narrower wins

The effective :mapping for a rendered layer is computed by merging, in order: root’s :mapping, then each ancestor composite’s :mapping, then the leaf’s own :mapping, then the layer’s own :mapping. Inner keys override outer. Any depth of composite nesting works the same way.

Root-level aesthetic flows to every leaf. Using a two-panel composite with :color declared at root:

(def s1-composite
  (pj/pose
   {:mapping {:color :species}
    :poses [{:mapping {:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width}
             :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}
            {:mapping {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}
             :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}]
    :data iris}))
s1-composite

Property P-S1 – sibling independence. A sub-pose’s own mapping does not leak into its siblings.

(def s1-siblings
  (pj/pose
   {:poses [{:mapping {:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width}
             :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}
            {:mapping {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width :color :species}
             :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}]
    :data iris}))
s1-siblings

Rule S2: data scope – nearest-ancestor-non-nil wins

The effective :data for a rendered layer is the nearest non-nil :data walking from the layer up through each ancestor to the root. Layer :data > leaf :data > nearest ancestor composite :data > root :data. Unlike mappings, data does not merge – it is picked, wholesale.

(def s2-tree
  (pj/pose
   {:poses [{:mapping {:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width}
             :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}
            {:mapping {:x :a :y :b}
             :layers [{:layer-type :point}]
             :data (tc/dataset {:a [1 2 3] :b [3 5 4]})}]
    :data iris}))
s2-tree

Rule S3: nil in a mapping cancels an inherited value

Assigning nil to a mapping key at an inner scope cancels the value inherited from outer scopes. The rendering path treats a nil mapping value as equivalent to “no mapping for that aesthetic.”

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/lay-smooth {:color nil :stat :linear-model}))

Rule S4: layer :mapping is the narrowest scope

A mapping written in a layer’s own :mapping (aesthetic mappings passed to lay-*) scopes to that layer only. Other layers – even on the same leaf – do not read that mapping. This is the terminal case of S1: the layer’s mapping is innermost in the merge.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/lay-point {:color :species})
    (pj/lay-smooth {:stat :linear-model}))

Rule S5: a row filter combines column by column at every level

A :where is a map from a column to the values kept, and each column is a separate condition. Where two filters meet, a column named in both takes the later or inner value, and columns named in one of them are kept as they are. A composite’s filter reaches every cell below it, a cell carrying data of its own included, as the composite’s mapping does.

Under a composite that keeps setosa, a cell naming versicolor draws versicolor; a cell naming a petal width keeps setosa too:

(-> iris
    (pj/pose {:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width :where {:species "setosa"}})
    (pj/arrange [{:where {:species "versicolor"}}
                 {:where {:petal-width 0.2}}])
    pj/lay-point)

The same two filters written with pj/pose, one after the other, give the same rows as the cell does:

(-> iris
    (pj/pose {:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width :where {:species "setosa"}})
    (pj/pose {:where {:species "versicolor"}})
    pj/lay-point)

Rule S6: a scale combines key by key, whichever function writes the mapping

A mapping value names one column and may carry a scale. Where two meet, the column is replaced and the scale settings combine key by key, as Scales describes. This holds for a layer under its pose, a cell under its composite, pj/scale, and pj/pose writing into a pose that already has a mapping – so a scale set before the columns are named reaches them:

(-> iris
    (pj/pose {})
    (pj/scale :x :log)
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pj/lay-point)

Options

Plot-level options and modifiers. Unlike mappings, layers, and data (which live in the scope hierarchy), options configure the whole rendered plot and attach to the root’s :opts.

Rule O1: pj/options writes to the root’s :opts

pj/options merges its argument into the current pose’s :opts. On a leaf, that is the leaf’s :opts. On a composite, the root’s. The root’s options reach every cell below it, and a cell’s own options win key by key (Rule O5); they configure panels and the plot, not layers.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/options {:title "Iris"}))

Repeated calls merge, later-wins on collisions:

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/options {:title "One"})
    (pj/options {:title "Two" :subtitle "Sub"}))

Rule O2: pj/scale writes the mapping, pj/coord writes options

A scale belongs to the aesthetic it reads, so pj/scale writes it into the pose’s :mapping, under that aesthetic’s :scale. It is the same key a mapping written out in full uses, so the two are one setting written two ways. pj/coord writes :coord into :opts, which has no aesthetic to belong to.

Axis aesthetics (:x, :y) accept :linear, :log, :categorical; the visual ones (:size, :alpha, :fill, :color) accept :linear and :log; :shape accepts :categorical. Both pj/scale and pj/coord flow down to every leaf beneath the pose they are called on.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/scale :x :log)
    (pj/coord :flip))

Where the aesthetic is already mapped, the scale joins that mapping. A mapping written plainly has no room for one, so it is rewritten in the full form under :from – the plain reading spelled out, which leaves what the mapping names unchanged:

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width {:size :petal-length})
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/scale :size :log))

Where it is not mapped at that pose, the scale is written on its own and applies to whatever names the aesthetic below:

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/lay-point {:size :petal-length})
    (pj/scale :size :log))

Rule O3: pj/facet writes a faceting column to the mapping, and a facet over columns to :facet

pj/facet writes the faceting column into the pose’s :mapping under :col, and a map {:col ... :row ...} writes both for a grid. These are aesthetics, so they follow the scope rules every other mapping follows: written on a pose they reach every layer and every sub-pose below, and a sub-pose that writes its own overrides them. The layout effect – splitting each leaf’s panel into a group of panels – happens at render time.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/facet :species))

A 2D grid uses both keys:

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/facet {:col :species :row :species}))

A grid crossing categories with columns keeps the two apart: the categories in the mapping, the columns under :facet. The two are crossed when the pose is drawn.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose {:x :sepal-length})
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/facet {:col :species :row {:y [:sepal-width :petal-width]}})
    (select-keys [:mapping :facet])
    kind/pprint)
{:mapping {:x :sepal-length, :col :species},
 :facet {:y [:sepal-width :petal-width]}}

Because the faceting column is a mapping, a facet written on a composite reaches every cell of it, and a cell that writes its own overrides what it inherits:

(-> (pj/arrange [(pj/pose iris :sepal-length :sepal-width)
                 (pj/pose iris :petal-length :petal-width)])
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/facet :species))
(-> (pj/arrange [(-> (pj/pose iris :sepal-length :sepal-width)
                     (pj/facet :species))
                 (pj/pose iris :petal-length :petal-width)])
    pj/lay-point)

A facet over columns is not a mapping. pj/facet given a map naming columns, such as {:y [:sepal-width :petal-width]}, keeps it under the pose’s :facet key, and the pose is expanded into a cell per column when it is drawn:

(-> iris
    (pj/pose {:x :sepal-length})
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/facet {:y [:sepal-width :petal-width]})
    pose-summary)
{:mapping {:x :sepal-length},
 :facet {:y [:sepal-width :petal-width]},
 :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}

Rule O4: pj/lay-rule-* and pj/lay-band-* are layers

pj/lay-rule-h, pj/lay-rule-v, pj/lay-band-h and pj/lay-band-v produce layers, and the layers are placed as any other lay-* layer is: a call naming no columns attaches at the root and is drawn in every panel, and on a composite a call naming two columns attaches to the leaf that draws them. On a pose with one panel, columns written on a rule or a band that the panel does not draw are not read: the rule is drawn on that panel, and a warning names the columns. Where the line or the band sits is written as layer-type keys (:y-intercept, :x-intercept, :y-min/:y-max, :x-min/:x-max), not as columns.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/lay-point {:color :species})
    (pj/lay-rule-h {:y-intercept 3.0}))

A rule naming two columns, on a composite, attaches to the leaf that draws them and is drawn in that leaf’s panel only:

(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
    (pj/lay-rule-h :sepal-length :sepal-width {:y-intercept 3.0}))

The same call on a pose with one panel draws the rule on that panel. The petal columns are not read, so the axes are those of the points:

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/lay-rule-h :petal-length :petal-width {:y-intercept 3.0}))
Notestdout 
Note: pj/lay-rule-h names :petal-length on :x and :petal-width on :y where this pose draws :sepal-length on :x and :sepal-width on :y, and is drawn on the same panel; in 0.16.1 it was given a panel of its own. For a panel per pair of columns, write (pj/facet pose {:x [:sepal-length :petal-length] :y [:sepal-width :petal-width]}), or arrange separate poses with pj/arrange.

Rule O5: a :theme combines key by key; other options are replaced

:theme and :config are maps of independent settings, so two of them combine key by key: pj/options twice, and a composite’s options reaching a cell that writes its own. Every other option is one value, replaced by the later or inner one – a :share-scales map included, since an axis it leaves out is not shared.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/options {:theme {:bg "#FFFFFF"}})
    (pj/options {:theme {:grid "#DDDDDD"}}))

A cell with a theme of its own keeps the composite’s background:

(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [(-> (pj/pose nil {:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width})
                     (pj/options {:theme {:grid "#DDDDDD"}}))
                 {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
    (pj/options {:theme {:bg "#FFFFFF"}})
    pj/lay-point)

Assembly

How the rules above combine to produce rendered layers. Each rendered layer corresponds to one (leaf, applicable-layer) pair, with all ancestor scope merged in.

Rule A1: one rendered layer per applicable (leaf, layer) pair

For each leaf, the rendered layers are the leaf’s own, plus each layer written above it whose layer type draws from as many columns as the leaf’s panel (Property P-LP1). A leaf drawing none of these has a layer inferred for it.

(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
    pj/lay-point                            ;; written on the root; reaches both
    (pj/lay-smooth :sepal-length :sepal-width
                   {:stat :linear-model}))  ;; written on sub-pose 1 only

Rule A2: each rendered layer carries fully merged scope

Every layer rendered in the final plot reflects the full scope merge: the dataset, every mapping that flows into it, :x and :y among them, and the layer-type bundle (plus any :stat, :position, :mark overrides). No scope level is dropped; no key is unresolved.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
    pj/lay-point)

Layout

How leaves become panels in the rendered plot. Five rules covering single panels, layers sharing a panel, faceting, composite grids with shared scales, and the scatter plot matrix.

Rule L1: each leaf produces a panel block

Each leaf produces one panel block in the rendered plot. Unfaceted, the block is one panel, which all of the leaf’s layers share (Rule LP5); pj/facet multiplies it by the facet values (or by the (row, col) pairs).

A facet over columns expands the leaf into one cell per column when the pose is drawn, so the plan of such a leaf holds :sub-plots, as the plan of a composite does.

(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
    pj/lay-point)

One leaf whose layers name two pairs of columns is one panel:

(-> iris
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width))
Notestdout 
Note: pj/lay-point names :petal-length on :x and :petal-width on :y where this pose draws :sepal-length on :x and :sepal-width on :y, and is drawn on the same panel; in 0.16.1 it was given a panel of its own. For a panel per pair of columns, write (pj/facet pose {:x [:sepal-length :petal-length] :y [:sepal-width :petal-width]}), or arrange separate poses with pj/arrange.

Rule L2: layers of a leaf overlay within its panel

Layers applicable to a leaf (the leaf’s own plus the layers written on the root that it draws) draw on the same axis pair – they overlay within the leaf’s panel, not on separate panels (Rule LP5).

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/lay-smooth {:stat :linear-model}))

Rule L3: faceting splits each leaf into panels, by category or by column

(pj/facet pose :species) draws one panel per distinct value of :species. On the mpg data, (pj/facet pose {:col :drv :row :cyl}) draws one panel per pair of values, the values of :drv across and the values of :cyl down. (pj/facet pose {:y [:hwy :cty]}) draws one panel per column (Rule O3). Each of the three takes a map of plot options as its last argument, which is the map pj/options takes.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/facet :species))

Rule L4: composite layout is controlled by :layout and optional :share-scales

A composite pose carries a :layout map, which holds the direction of its rows and, in each row, the direction of the cells. pj/arrange writes :title, :width, :height and :share-scales into the composite’s :opts, and :cols into its :layout (Rule C8). An optional :share-scales (a subset of #{:x :y}, or a map from an axis to :same-column, :all, or groups of columns) enables shared-scale resolution across sub-poses. Under a set, sharing is column-bucketed.

Column-bucketing: when :x is shared, sub-poses whose effective :x column is the same share that scale’s domain; sub-poses with different :x columns get independent x-domains. Same for :y. Marginal plots rest on this: a top strip draws the scatter’s :x column on the horizontal axis and shares :x with the scatter. A right strip is drawn with :coord :flip, so the scatter’s :y column runs up the strip’s vertical axis, and the strip and the scatter share :y. In :share-scales, :x is the horizontal axis and :y the vertical axis, also for a panel drawn with :coord :flip. A count or density axis is shared among the cells that compute the same thing from the same column.

(def l4-shared
  (pj/arrange
   [(-> iris (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width) pj/lay-point)
    (-> iris (pj/pose :sepal-length :petal-width) pj/lay-point)]
   {:share-scales #{:x}}))
l4-shared

Rule L5: a facet crossing two lists of columns has one panel per pair

(pj/facet data {:col {:x xs} :row {:y ys}}) returns a leaf pose – no :poses – that carries that facet map: a column of the grid for each column of xs, a row for each column of ys, and a panel where they cross. Its axes, tick labels and strips are a facet’s (Rule L3). The same list in both places is a scatter plot matrix.

A panel with one column on both axes draws a histogram of that column, and every other panel draws the layer type inferred for its two columns – a scatter for two numerical columns. A layer added with pj/lay-* is drawn in the panels whose number of columns its layer type draws from, so pj/lay-point after the facet leaves the histograms on the diagonal (Property P-LP1). pj/pose given pairs of columns reports an error that suggests pj/arrange and pj/matrix, which writes this facet.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose {:color :species})
    (pj/facet {:col {:x [:sepal-length :sepal-width]}
              :row {:y [:petal-length :petal-width]}}))

A Note on pj/cross

pj/cross is deprecated, and calling it prints a warning. It returns the pairs (for [x xs y ys] [x y]), and a pair of columns is not a cell of pj/arrange, where a vector is a list of cells. For a panel for every column of xs crossed with every column of ys, write (pj/matrix data xs ys), which writes the facet of Rule L5:

(-> iris
    (pj/matrix [:sepal-length :sepal-width] [:petal-length :petal-width])
    pj/lay-point)

For a panel per pair of columns chosen one by one, write each pair as a mapping, as in Rule C8.
